title: Canva API: How the Connect API Works (2026 Guide)
summary: Canva API requires OAuth authentication, not static keys. Every call needs user authorization, so decide whose permissions your workflow will borrow.
body_markdown:
## Get Canva API access and credentials


Access starts with registering an integration in the Developer Portal. Connect issues no static key, so you declare the integration's scopes and redirect URL and then collect a client ID and client secret.


### Create a Canva integration in the Developer Portal


Sign in to Canva's Developer Portal and create a new integration. Before you do, confirm in Canva's developer documentation which plan the account needs for Connect API access, because the plan belongs to the account that owns the integration.


Decide who that owner is now. An integration created under a contractor's personal login is the one that breaks when that person leaves, and the client secret goes with it.


### Choose scopes and set the redirect URL


Scopes are the permissions your integration may request from a user, such as reading design metadata or reading assets. Select only what the workflow needs.


> An integration created under a contractor's personal login is the one that breaks when that person leaves, and the client secret goes with it.


Every scope you list appears on the consent screen, and a token can never do more than the scopes it was granted. If you add a scope later, users who already connected must authorize again.


When a first authorization attempt fails, a redirect URL mismatch is the most common reason.


The redirect URL is the address Canva sends the user back to with an authorization code, and it must match exactly what your application sends during authorization, including scheme, host and path. Copy the value from your configuration rather than retyping it.


### Get your Canva client ID and secret


The client ID identifies your integration and can sit in configuration. The client secret's a credential: generate it, store it straight into a secrets manager, and never put it in front-end code or a repository.


If the secret's exposed or lost, generate a replacement rather than trying to recover it, and update every system that holds the old one.


Neither value's a bearer token. They're what you exchange, together with the authorization code, for access and refresh tokens.


A no-code builder wraps that exchange in a single connection.


The flow below sends new HubSpot tickets (HubSpot is a customer-relationship platform) through two AI steps and a router to three Slack messages. It shows where that connection lives: the trigger's Connection field, which every later step uses.


Whoever authorizes that connection is the identity the flow acts as, so authorize it with an account the team controls.


With the client ID, the secret, the scopes and the redirect URL recorded and assigned to a named owner, the next job is the authorization exchange itself. That exchange also covers handling the tokens it returns.
